First-Generation College Student (FGCS): A student in the first generation of their family to go to college (i.e., a student whose parents/guardians/caregivers did not earn bachelor’s degrees, although elder siblings and cousins may be attending college already or have earned four-year degrees). title: What's The Word?
description: Description: “What’s the Word?” is a facilitated conversation and community-building space for men of colour at Boston University. The event is designed to provide a welcoming and supportive environment where students can openly discuss topics and experiences that affect their communities, including campus life, identity, personal development, relationships, academics, and professional growth. Through guided discussions and informal conversation, participants will have the opportunity to build fellowship and camaraderie, develop meaningful connections, and foster mentorship between members of the community. The overall goal of “What’s the Word?” is to create a space where men of colour at BU can feel comfortable sharing their perspectives, supporting one another, building a stronger sense of belonging, and developing lasting connections within the university community. How is this event aligned with Howard Thurman’s philosophies? “What’s the Word?” aligns closely with Howard Thurman’s philosophy of searching for common ground through self-understanding, meaningful dialogue, and genuine connection with others. The event creates a space centred on the experiences of men of colour and other underrepresented communities at Boston University, where students can openly discuss topics affecting their identities, communities, relationships, academic experiences, and personal development. Through these conversations, attendees are encouraged to better understand their own experiences while also listening to and learning from the perspectives of others. In doing so, the event promotes fellowship, empathy, mentorship, and a stronger sense of community, reflecting Thurman’s belief that meaningful shared experiences can help overcome the barriers that separate people. How will it create an experience of self-exploration and connection for the attendees? This event will create opportunities for self-exploration through guided and open-ended conversations that encourage participants to reflect on their identities, experiences, challenges, goals, and roles within their communities. Attendees will have opportunities to share their perspectives while hearing from others who may have similar or different experiences. These discussions are intended not only to encourage personal reflection, but also to help students recognise common experiences and develop meaningful relationships. This directly reflects the Howard Thurman Centre’s emphasis on discovering oneself through interaction and connection with others. How will the event organiser attract a reasonable amount of attendees to fill the space being requested? We will promote these events through social media, group chats, flyers, word of mouth, and outreach to other student organisations and affinity groups. By combining broad campus promotion with personal outreach from members, Brothers United aims to reach students beyond its current membership and encourage strong participation in the event.

title: First-Gen Support Group
description: This group offers a safe and supportive space for students who identify as a first-generation college student. Topics discussed may include navigating unfamiliar situations, balancing academics with social life, managing responsibilities and finances, and processing feelings, such as excitement, guilt, shame, confusion and pride. The group emphasizes building community supports and sharing resources. The group is lead by a licensed clinical social worker, Rashidat, who was a first-generation college graduate along with a first-gen graduate student in a BU counseling program. What does it mean to be first-generation at Boston University? First-Generation College Student (FGCS): A student in the first generation of their family to go to college (i.e., a student whose parents/guardians/caregivers did not earn bachelor’s degrees, although elder siblings and cousins may be attending college already or have earned four-year degrees). First-Generation Graduate/Professional Student (FGGS/FGPS): A student who is in the first-generation of their families to pursue an advanced degree (i.e., a student whose parents/guardians/caregivers did not earn a master’s, doctorate, or professional degree, such as a JD or MD).

title: Earn Success
description: This program will focus on promoting educational advancement, mentorship, and academic achievement while following the Go-To-High-School, Go-To-College and Educational Support & Advocacy initiatives. The program will encourage attendees to become advocates for education and provide resources to support future generations of scholars. Attendees will discuss the importance of mentorship and representation in helping students navigate educational pathways. Attendees will apply their knowledge of the college preparation process while learning about resources they can share with future students.

title: Red Star Theater's Fall 2026 Performance — Suspect Zero
description: This Fall 2026, Red Star Theater proudly presents Suspect Zero (0号嫌疑人). A violent storm. A mysterious murder. Six people, each with something to hide. When a wealthy man is found dead in his villa, six people find themselves trapped under the same roof. As secrets come to light and suspicions grow, everyone becomes a suspect. Who is telling the truth? Who has something to hide? And who is the real killer? Blending mystery, comedy, and unexpected twists, Suspect Zero takes audiences on a thrilling journey full of secrets, laughter, and surprises. Created and performed by Boston University students, Suspect Zero invites you to follow the clues, question everyone, and uncover the truth.

title: Homecoming Party (COPY)
description: The purpose of SoulAAn’s Homecoming Party is to build community, school spirit, and cultural connection by creating a fun and welcoming space where students can come together, celebrate, and feel connected to BU. Although BU does not have a traditional football-centered homecoming experience, this event gives students an opportunity to still experience BU pride, participate in a campus tradition, and celebrate homecoming in a way that reflects Black culture, music, and community. For many students, especially Black students and students from underrepresented communities, events like this help make campus feel more welcoming, lively, and connected.Funding this event is important because the atmosphere of a homecoming party depends heavily on music, energy, and intentional programming. Our DJ would also not just serve background music for this event; the DJ helps guide the flow of the night, keep students engaged, and create a safe and organized party environment, to make the event feel like a real homecoming celebration rather than just a room rental. The requested funding would allow us to provide quality music and entertainment, decorate the space, and create an experience that encourages students to build relationships, show school pride, and feel represented in campus life. This event would also help SoulAAn establish a new tradition for BU students who may not otherwise feel connected to traditional homecoming culture. By investing in this event, the university would be supporting student belonging, cultural celebration, and community-building across campus and the greater Boston intercollegiate Black community.

title: BUCD Hosts Voter Registration Day
description: Boston University College Democrats wants to host a day-long tabling event encouraging people to register to vote and informing them of different voting laws depending on the states they are from. description: Description: “What’s the Word?” is a facilitated conversation and community-building space for men of colour at Boston University. Through guided discussions and informal conversation, participants will have the opportunity to build fellowship and camaraderie, develop meaningful connections, and foster mentorship between members of the community. title: First-Gen Support Group
description: This group offers a safe and supportive space for students who identify as a first-generation college student. Topics discussed may include navigating unfamiliar situations, balancing academics with social life, managing responsibilities and finances, and processing feelings, such as excitement, guilt, shame, confusion and pride. The group emphasizes building community supports and sharing resources. The group is lead by a licensed clinical social worker, Rashidat, who was a first-generation college graduate along with a first-gen graduate student in a BU counseling program. What does it mean to be first-generation at Boston University? First-Generation College Student (FGCS): A student in the first generation of their family to go to college (i.e., a student whose parents/guardians/caregivers did not earn bachelor’s degrees, although elder siblings and cousins may be attending college already or have earned four-year degrees). First-Generation Graduate/Professional Student (FGGS/FGPS): A student who is in the first-generation of their families to pursue an advanced degree (i.e., a student whose parents/guardians/caregivers did not earn a master’s, doctorate, or professional degree, such as a JD or MD).

title: First-Gen Support Group
description: This group offers a safe and supportive space for students who identify as a first-generation college student. Topics discussed may include navigating unfamiliar situations, balancing academics with social life, managing responsibilities and finances, and processing feelings, such as excitement, guilt, shame, confusion and pride. The group emphasizes building community supports and sharing resources. The group is lead by a licensed clinical social worker, Rashidat, who was a first-generation college graduate along with a first-gen graduate student in a BU counseling program. What does it mean to be first-generation at Boston University? First-Generation College Student (FGCS): A student in the first generation of their family to go to college (i.e., a student whose parents/guardians/caregivers did not earn bachelor’s degrees, although elder siblings and cousins may be attending college already or have earned four-year degrees). First-Generation Graduate/Professional Student (FGGS/FGPS): A student who is in the first-generation of their families to pursue an advanced degree (i.e., a student whose parents/guardians/caregivers did not earn a master’s, doctorate, or professional degree, such as a JD or MD).

title: Elections Midterm Watch Party
description: The midterms watch party hosted by Student Governments City Affairs Department will have a live streaming of a news broadcast that shows midterm polling and coverage across the country. There will be catering onsite as well for students to eat as they watch as well as a fun interactive bingo sheets that students can mark off as votes roll in. Stickers would be handed out for students who attend. It is a way to round off Terrier Turnout Week 2026 and help students become politically literate and bond over democracy.

title: What's The Word?
description: Description: “What’s the Word?” is a facilitated conversation and community-building space for men of colour at Boston University. The event is designed to provide a welcoming and supportive environment where students can openly discuss topics and experiences that affect their communities, including campus life, identity, personal development, relationships, academics, and professional growth. Through guided discussions and informal conversation, participants will have the opportunity to build fellowship and camaraderie, develop meaningful connections, and foster mentorship between members of the community. The overall goal of “What’s the Word?” is to create a space where men of colour at BU can feel comfortable sharing their perspectives, supporting one another, building a stronger sense of belonging, and developing lasting connections within the university community. How is this event aligned with Howard Thurman’s philosophies? “What’s the Word?” aligns closely with Howard Thurman’s philosophy of searching for common ground through self-understanding, meaningful dialogue, and genuine connection with others. The event creates a space centred on the experiences of men of colour and other underrepresented communities at Boston University, where students can openly discuss topics affecting their identities, communities, relationships, academic experiences, and personal development. Through these conversations, attendees are encouraged to better understand their own experiences while also listening to and learning from the perspectives of others. In doing so, the event promotes fellowship, empathy, mentorship, and a stronger sense of community, reflecting Thurman’s belief that meaningful shared experiences can help overcome the barriers that separate people. How will it create an experience of self-exploration and connection for the attendees? This event will create opportunities for self-exploration through guided and open-ended conversations that encourage participants to reflect on their identities, experiences, challenges, goals, and roles within their communities. Attendees will have opportunities to share their perspectives while hearing from others who may have similar or different experiences. These discussions are intended not only to encourage personal reflection, but also to help students recognise common experiences and develop meaningful relationships. This directly reflects the Howard Thurman Centre’s emphasis on discovering oneself through interaction and connection with others. How will the event organiser attract a reasonable amount of attendees to fill the space being requested? We will promote these events through social media, group chats, flyers, word of mouth, and outreach to other student organisations and affinity groups. By combining broad campus promotion with personal outreach from members, Brothers United aims to reach students beyond its current membership and encourage strong participation in the event.
